preserved_objections.basis: Wavelet decomposition is fundamentally a signal processing technique designed for stationary or quasi-stationary signals, while retail demand exhibits strong non-stationarity due to seasonality, promotions, and external events. The candidate provides no evidence that wavelets can effectively isolate temporal patterns in this highly irregular context.

No boundary conditions are specified, making it impossible to determine if this approach would work across different retail categories (perishable vs. durable), geographic regions, or time periods. The claim of "within 7 days at or above 15% WAPE inflation" is completely unsubstantiated without defined operational boundaries.

The cited evidence bundle contains zero studies on wavelet decomposition for retail forecasting. The references include building energy prediction, pharmaceutical supply chains, abrasive wear optimization, and blood donor profiling—none of which are relevant to retail demand forecasting or feature drift detection.

The candidate fails to explain how wavelet decomposition would outperform simpler, more interpretable approaches like exponential smoothing or moving averages that are already standard in retail forecasting. There's no theoretical or empirical basis for why this complex method would perform better than the baseline.

The candidate proposes a novel design variable but provides no details about implementation. Wavelet decomposition requires careful selection of mother wavelets, decomposition levels, and thresholding methods—all of which would need extensive tuning for retail data that the candidate doesn't address.

The testable prediction compares "time-to-detection" but doesn't specify how drift severity is measured, what constitutes a "detection," or how false positives/negatives will be handled. The 15% WAPE inflation threshold is arbitrary without justification for why this specific threshold matters operationally.
